title: Washington dance, segregation in the South, and drummer Charlie Buck quits
summary: With a white drummer unable to go South, Malachi brings in Charlie Buck, who flees back to Washington after meeting Jim Crow at Rocky Mount.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Anyway, we made this dance that night, and this was our first dance in Wilmington, Delaware. The next one was in Washington, D.C., and I think it was at Turner's Arena up at Fourteenth and W Streets. We played this dance, and now everybody's wondering what's going to happen, because at that particular time, no White musician was allowed to play with a Black musician below Washington, D.C. And our schedule was... Our next dance was to be at the June German, a Festival they had down there every year (I don't know if they still have it
or not) in Rocky Mountain, North Carolina. They had three bands down there. It was Buddy Johnson, and a band from California that you mentioned....

I think it was Buddy Johnson and Les Hite and Billy Eckstine. They played in this huge tobacco warehouse, and they had three big bands there. But in Washington, after this dance, we were wondering "What we gonna do?" you know. You know, we have no drummer. So I told them about this drummer that I knew that was playing at the Crystal Caverns, when I was up with Trummy, and he was a an excellent drummer and a very good reader -- just a good drummer all the way around. His name was... Everybody called him Charlie Buck. And I went and got him to join the band, and he went down and played this dance with us in Rocky Mountain, North Carolina. But Charlie had a young lady back here in Washington, D.C. that he was very much in love with, and he got into Rocky Mountain, North Carolina, and I guess he got to thinking about her. And he came to, me and told me, "Mal, I think I'm going back to Washington." Because he'd never been South before, and when we got down there... Washington, D.C. was segregated enough then, but when he got down to Rocky Mountain, North Carolina, he really found out what segregation was like, with the two toilets and all this mess in the station.

So after the dance that night, he comes up with this (everybody knew it was a lie)...that his old lady had just called him and told him that the draft board said that he had to come to Washington right away. So he went and told Billy Eckstine, and Billy said, "Well, you know that's true." He swears... So in the meantime... It was a funny thing. It's the only time that I have ever seen Charlie Parker or Dizzy Gillespie beg somebody to play. Because all of our engagements were due South, and the chances of finding a drummer down there was next to none! Imagine a 17-piece band trying to swing with no drummer. Nevertheless, Charlie Buck stood fast, caught the next train back to Washington, and left us without a drummer.
